body.text: Why does Subdivisions of the Democratic Republic of the Congo still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism that quietly governs liquidity, risk, and long-term purchasing power.

The Third Republic of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a unitary state with a five-level hierarchy of types of administrative division. There are nine different types of country subdivision in a new hierarchy with no new types but with two from the previous one abolished.

Under the Third Republic, established in 2006, the number of provinces has gone from ten to twenty-five. By fits and starts the number of towns that have been, or are in the process of being, upgraded to cities has also increased greatly.

Reforms to devolve powers to the provinces were completed in 2006, but devolution to more local levels have again been delayed when elections scheduled for 2019 were not held. Traditional authority continues to play a significant role in governance with traditional leaders leading many of the subdivisions at the lower levels.

body.text: History of decentralization

According to Christian Mulemndeko Namegabe of the Institut Supérieur de Développement Rural de Bukavu (ISDR-Bukavu), the territorial administration in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has gone through six main periods since independence. Between 1960 and 1966, the country experimented with federalism.

This was followed by a period of strong centralization from 1966 to 1977, when power was mainly held by the central government. From 1977 to 1982, the government began making changes to support decentralization. However, between 1982 and 1990, decentralization took place under a one-party system.

Then, from 1990 to 1997, it continued as the country moved toward multiparty politics. Since 1997, territorial administration has become more divided because of foreign military forces and rebel groups governing some areas. Mulemndeko points out that the Constitution adopted on 18 February 2006 included plans for administrative decentralization.
Even so, the plan required laws to explain how it should be carried out, and it has still not been put into effect.
Under the first republic

During the First Republic, the country faced many problems within its institutions, and, as a result, provincial matters were often managed separately, with little coordination at the national level. Efforts to restore state authority nationwide led to greater centralization of power.

North Katanga was established under the law of 27 April 1962, followed by 15 additional provinces on 14 August 1962. In 1963, five more provinces were established: Middle Congo (Moyen Congo), Upper Congo (Haut-Congo), Central Kivu, Lualaba, and Eastern Katanga (Katanga Oriental). The legal status of Léopoldville was established on 10 October 1962.
Ordinance-Law No. 82/006 of 25 February 1982 and its rationale

Before 1982, decentralization remained incomplete. Its implementation was selective, benefiting only a limited number of territorial entities. Other entities remained under centralized control, with varying degrees of administrative deconcentration. Against this backdrop, the MPR Central Committee, at its second ordinary session (March, June 1981), resolved to revive the decentralization program.

Known as the Vunalawe Law (Loi Vunalawe), Law No. 82/006 of 25 February 1982 was based on four speeches by President Mobutu Sese Seko concerning the revolution, delivered on 1 July 1977, 25 July 1987, 19 November 1980, and 26 March 1981. According to Mulemndeko, two considerations were central to the rationale for decentralization.

First, Mobutu argued that decentralization had initially been necessary to restore state authority, maintain peace, promote national cohesion, and preserve territorial integrity. However, he also warned that keeping too much power at the central level for too long could weaken the country's political, administrative, and economic systems.
Second, he noticed that fewer people were taking part in party activities and that public opinion was not receiving enough attention.

The 1982 reform was therefore a major step in the history of territorial decentralization, as it recognized that regions, cities, and local communities had their own needs and interests, which had to be considered alongside the duties of the central government.
As a result, the law set up local bodies to take care of these interests.

Earlier laws mainly focused on how the state and its administrative areas were organized. 80-006 of 25 February 1982 introduced territorial decentralization in both urban and rural areas to bring party members closer to the administration so that development in their entities could be better planned.

The law gave each decentralized territorial entity (entité territoriale décentralisée, or ETD) general authority over its local affairs. The law also set out the duties that local entities could manage in areas such as administration, the economy, social affairs, and culture. At the same time, it identified the responsibilities that remained with the central government.

This helped divide public duties between the state and its local entities. To make this system work, each level had a body responsible for discussing and deciding on local issues. Each region and the city of Kinshasa had a regional assembly, while other decentralized entities had councils.
These bodies also checked the work of the regional and local executive leaders to ensure that they managed their responsibilities properly.

Each ETD had an executive body responsible for carrying out decisions and managing its daily activities. The law gave these duties to bodies that already represented the central government in different regions. Instead of creating new bodies, the law gave the existing ones an additional role.

This meant that they had two responsibilities at the same time, and, as a result, the regional governor (gouverneur de la région), zone commissioner (commissaire de zone), and chief of the collectivité (chef de collectivité) acted as representatives of the central government and as leaders of their respective ETDs.

Although decentralization gave local entities more power, the Republic of Zaire remained a unitary state, and therefore, national unity and respect for the law still had to be maintained. To achieve this, the law gave the central government the power to supervise bodies at all levels of the country's territory.

Depending on the situation, this supervision could be carried out through hierarchical control, administrative supervision (tutelle), or the courts. Hierarchical control involved supervision by higher authorities over lower ones. Administrative supervision allowed the central government to monitor ETD bodies and the decisions they made.
Members of the public had the right to challenge decisions made by administrative authorities before the courts responsible for handling such cases.
Changes introduced by the 1982 Law

First, the decentralization system introduced in 1982 applied to all major territorial entities in urban and rural areas. Instead of having separate laws for different areas, the law brought them together under one legal framework.
This ended the two-part system inherited from colonial rule, which had remained in place since the Decree of 12 January 1923 concerning urban districts.

The second change was the creation of regional and local assemblies for the five types of ETDs, including regions, urban zones (villes zones urbaines), rural zones (zones rurales), and collectivités. These assemblies serve as deliberative bodies and provide ongoing oversight of the management of regional or local authorities.

The third change was that the power to organize territorial entities was given exclusively to the president of the republic. Article 39 of the Constitution gave the president the duty of protecting the country's territorial integrity.

Because of this change, the State Commissioner, also known as the Minister responsible for Territorial Administration, lost the power to organize basic territorial entities such as collectivités, towns (cités), quartiers (quarters), groupings (groupements), and localities (localités).

The fourth change was the introduction of territorial entities that were different from those under the previous law, which followed the reform of 10 April 1967. The 1982 law introduced new definitions for cities, groupings, quarters, and localities, changing how these entities were understood and organized.

A city was defined as a regional capital or any important urban entity that was given city status by the president of the republic through an official order. However, this decision had to follow clear legal conditions. The law also gave a new meaning to the cité.
It referred either to the administrative center of a subregion or rural zone, or to an urban settlement with at least 15,000 people and a large number of workers.
